posts.post_title: Which term denotes seeing a carcass, used in veterinary…

Necropsy is the term used in veterinary medicine for seeing/examining a carcass.

The term literally means seeing a carcass and is applied specifically to animal postmortem examination, distinguishing it from human autopsy.

  • Autopsy means seeing with one's own eyes and is the term used in human medicine, not veterinary medicine.

Know More
  • Pathology (Gr.) means study/discourse of disease.

  • Clinical pathology aids diagnosis at the patient's bedside.

posts.post_title: In a herd of 100 exposed animals, 60 became affected…
posts.post_content: In a herd of 100 animals exposed to a disease, 60 animals became affected. What is the morbidity rate?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 60%

Morbidity is the percentage of exposed animals that become affected.

Correct Option Explanation

With 100 animals exposed and 60 affected, morbidity is calculated as (60/100) × 100 = 60%.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 30% does not correspond to the ratio of affected to exposed animals given.
  • 50% is not the correct ratio for 60 affected out of 100 exposed.
  • 100% would mean all exposed animals were affected, which is not the case here.
Know More
  • Mortality rate is percentage of deaths among affected animals.
  • Morbidity and mortality are key epidemiological indices in disease study.
  • Prognosis estimates probable severity and outcome of disease.
  • Disease is any deviation from normal structure or function.

  • Morbidity is percentage of exposed animals that become affected.
  • Termination of disease is recovery, death, or prolonged chronicity.
  • Incubation period lapses between cause and manifestation of disease.
  • Differential diagnosis differentiates a disease from other diseases.

posts.post_title: Haemorrhages at the base of the pulmonary artery and…

posts.post_title: Naming the actual cause of a disease, such as bacteria…
posts.post_content: When a disease like pneumonia is diagnosed by identifying its actual cause, such as bacteria, virus, fungus or foreign body, this is termed which type of diagnosis?

posts.post_title: Rinderpest occurring in cattle but not in other…
posts.post_content: Rinderpest occurring in cattle but not in other animal species illustrates which type of predisposing cause of disease?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Species

Species is a predisposing cause; rinderpest is found in cattle but not other animals.

Correct Option Explanation

Predisposing (intrinsic) causes make an animal susceptible to definitive causes; species-specific susceptibility is illustrated by rinderpest affecting only cattle.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Breed susceptibility is illustrated instead by heavier dog breeds suffering more from bone diseases.

  • Colour predisposition includes sunburn in melanin-deficient skin.

  • Idiosyncrasy is a different drug reaction between animals.

posts.post_title: Pompe's disease, involving lysosomal acid maltase…
posts.post_content: Pompe's disease, a lysosomal acid maltase deficiency reported in cattle and dogs, is an example of which predisposing cause of disease?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

posts.post_title: Which inorganic chemical among the definitive causes…

posts.post_title: A wound involving tearing of tissues, typically seen…

posts.post_title: A joint injury in which anatomical relationship of…

posts.post_title: A female calf with arrested development of sex organs…

posts.post_title: Increased volume of blood in an affected tissue or…
posts.post_content: Increased volume of blood in an affected tissue or part is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Hyperaemia

Hyperaemia is defined as increased volume of blood in the affected tissue or part.

Hyperaemia may be active (arterial, due to increased blood flow) or passive/congestion (venous, due to impaired drainage).

  • Active hyperaemia occurs in arterioles or arteries.

posts.post_title: Congestion, resulting from impaired venous drainage…

posts.post_title: Which of the following is a physiological cause of…
posts.post_content: Which of the following is cited as a physiological cause of acute local active hyperaemia?

posts.post_title: Increase in size/weight with a mottled, dark-red and…

posts.post_title: Accumulation of blood in the ventral portions of the…

posts.post_title: Bleeding from the nose is termed which of the…

posts.post_title: Mucopolysaccharidosis type I, caused by absence of…

posts.post_title: Caspase-3 and caspase-6 are functionally classified…

posts.post_title: Aggregation of chromatin under the nuclear membrane…

posts.post_title: Which of the following processes of cell death…

posts.post_title: Black or dark-green discolouration of putrefying…

posts.post_title: The postmortem stage characterized by cooling of the…
posts.post_content: The postmortem stage characterized by cooling of the body, commencing at or before the stoppage of blood flow, is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

Algor mortis is cooling of the body after death.

Its rate depends on atmospheric temperature, air currents, hair coat thickness, adiposity and gut contents.

  • Rigor mortis is contraction of muscles after death, a separate, later postmortem stage.

posts.post_title: Contraction of muscles after death, causing joints to…
posts.post_content: Contraction of muscles after death, causing joints to become stiff and the body to become rigid, is termed which of the following?

posts.post_title: Onset of rigor mortis is delayed in animals having…
posts.post_content: Onset of rigor mortis is delayed in well-fed animals having large quantities of stored what, within their muscles?

  • ATP breakdown without resynthesis is the underlying cause of rigor.
  • Relaxation of muscle requires absorption of ATP by muscle proteins.
  • High atmospheric temperature also hastens the onset of rigor mortis.

posts.post_title: Yellow pigmentation of tissue occurring in the…

posts.post_title: Dry gangrene, unlike moist gangrene, is characterized…

posts.post_title: Tattoo pigments, deposited in the dermis for animal…

posts.post_title: Which of the following groups is noted to store little…

posts.post_title: Deposition of lead in chronic poisoning, producing a…
posts.post_content: Deposition of lead in chronic poisoning, producing a blue line along the gum and grey faeces, is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Plumbism

Plumbism is deposition of lead in the body during chronic poisoning.

Correct Option Explanation

Lead sulphide, formed from hydrogen sulphide and lead, produces a characteristic blue line in the gum and along tooth edges.

  • Argyria is instead deposition of silver, causing grayish-blue discolouration of skin, not a gum line.

  • Sources of lead include grains, water, fodder and lead batteries.
  • Hydrogen sulphide for the reaction derives from putrefaction of food particles.
  • Argyria pigment deposits are extracellular, in dermis and vessel walls.

posts.post_title: Deposition of silver as a finely granular albuminate…
posts.post_content: Deposition of silver as a finely granular albuminate in tissue, producing grayish-blue discolouration of skin and conjunctiva, is termed which of the following?

Argyria is deposition of silver as finely granular albuminate in tissue.

  • Plumbism is instead lead deposition, producing a blue line in the gum, not silver-related skin discolouration.

  • Argyria involves internal organs as well as skin and conjunctiva.
  • The pigment is extracellular, deposited in dermis and vessel walls.

posts.post_title: Melanin is produced by oxidation of tyrosine via…
posts.post_content: Melanin is produced by oxidation of tyrosine to dihydroxy phenyl alanine via which copper-containing enzyme in the melanocyte?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Tyrosinase

Tyrosinase, a copper-containing enzyme, oxidises tyrosine to form melanin.

Correct Option Explanation

This enzyme acts within melanocytes located in the basal epidermis, retina, iris and pia-arachnoid, converting tyrosine via DOPA.

  • Myeloperoxidase is instead a neutrophil enzyme involved in bacterial killing, unrelated to pigment synthesis.

  • Hyaluronidase is a tumour-associated enzyme that hydrolyses cementing substance, unrelated to melanin synthesis.

  • Melanin protects the skin from ultraviolet radiation.
  • Albinism results from lack of tyrosinase despite normal-appearing melanocytes.
  • Melanocytes give a DOPA-positive reaction, while melanophores are DOPA-negative.
  • Grey horses are especially susceptible to melanoma.

posts.post_title: Melanin deficiency due to lack of tyrosinase, despite…
posts.post_content: Melanin deficiency due to lack of tyrosinase, despite melanocytes appearing normal in number, is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Albinism

Albinism is melanin deficiency due to lack of tyrosinase, with normal-appearing melanocytes.

Lack of pigmentation in skin, hair, sclera or iris on sunlight exposure may predispose affected animals to skin cancer.

  • Leukoderma is instead local loss of skin pigment, e.g. under a collar or harness, not enzyme-based.

Know More
  • Copper deficiency in cattle and sheep also causes loss of coat colour.
  • Melanosis may occur in the intestine, heart, lung and kidney.
  • Corneal melanosis in Boxers and Western Terriers may cause blindness.
  • Macrophages laden with melanin are called melanophores.

posts.post_title: The pigment described as the 'aging pigment' or…
posts.post_content: The pigment described as the 'aging pigment' or 'wear and tear pigment', accumulating in post-mitotic cells like neurons and cardiomyocytes, is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lipofuscin

Lipofuscin is known as the aging pigment or wear and tear pigment.

Correct Option Explanation

This brownish-yellow, intracellular pigment accumulates in post-mitotic cells such as neurons, cardiomyocytes and skeletal myocytes, causing brown atrophy.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Ceroid is instead described as an early, pathological form of lipofuscin, not the general aging pigment itself.
  • Melanin is a black pigment from tyrosine oxidation, unrelated to aging-related cellular pigment accumulation.
  • Haemosiderin is derived from haemoglobin breakdown, unrelated to the aging pigment concept.
Know More
  • Lipofuscin cannot be removed by lysosomal degradation or exocytosis.
  • The pigment shows fat-soluble, acid-fast and PAS-positive histochemistry.
  • Ceroid occurs in severe malnutrition, including hypovitaminosis E.
  • Haemosiderin is greatest in the horse spleen and least in the dog spleen.

posts.post_title: Calcification of soft tissue occurring due to a rise…
posts.post_content: Calcification of soft tissue occurring due to a rise in blood calcium (hypercalcaemia) is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Metastatic calcification

Metastatic calcification is deposition of calcium in soft tissue following hypercalcaemia.

Correct Option Explanation

Causes include parathyroid tumour, primary/secondary bone tumours, high vitamin D intake, and renal disease with phosphate retention.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Dystrophic calcification instead occurs in abnormal/necrotic tissue with normal blood calcium levels.
  • Haemochromatosis is extreme accumulation of iron, an unrelated mineral-storage disease.
  • Amyloidosis is deposition of an abnormal glycoprotein (amyloid), not calcium salts.
Know More
  • Parathyroid tumours cause hyperphosphaturia and hypophosphataemia.
  • Renal disease causes phosphate retention and parathyroid stimulation.
  • Calcium deposits wherever acid is secreted, e.g. stomach and kidney.
  • Dystrophic calcification examples include TB lesions and old thrombi.

posts.post_title: Calcification of necrotic or abnormal tissue…
posts.post_content: Calcification of necrotic or abnormal tissue occurring with normal blood calcium levels is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Dystrophic calcification

Dystrophic calcification occurs in abnormal tissue with normal blood calcium levels.

Correct Option Explanation

Examples include tuberculous lesions, suppurative lesions, scar tissue, dead parasites, atherosclerotic plaques and old thrombi.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Metastatic calcification instead requires elevated blood calcium (hypercalcaemia), unlike this condition.
  • Gout is deposition of uric acid and urates in tissue, a different mineral entirely.
  • Hyaline degeneration is a glassy tissue appearance unrelated to calcium salt deposition.
Know More
  • Phosphates from dead tissue form the nidus for calcium deposition.
  • Calcium combines with phosphates to form calcium soaps.
  • Gross lesions are hard, gritty masses, often microscopic in size.
  • Calcified areas stain blue with H&E and black with von Kossa stain.

posts.post_title: In the stomach, wherever acid is secreted, calcium…
posts.post_content: In the stomach, wherever acid is secreted, calcium deposition tends to occur. Which acid is specifically responsible for this in the stomach?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: HCl

Hydrochloric acid (HCl) secretion in the stomach is associated with calcium deposition there.

Correct Option Explanation

The principle that calcium deposits wherever acid is secreted applies organ-specifically: stomach with HCl, kidney with hippuric acid, lungs with CO2.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Hippuric acid is instead the acid cited for calcium deposition in the kidneys, not the stomach.
  • Uric acid is the end product of protein metabolism in birds, unrelated to this calcification principle.
  • Lactic acid is associated with tumour cell metabolism and infiltration, not this calcification principle.
Know More
  • CO2 is the acid-related factor cited for calcium deposition in lungs.
  • Dystrophic calcification occurs at sites of normal blood calcium levels.
  • Metastatic calcification instead requires hypercalcaemia.
  • Nutritional causes of hypercalcaemia include high vitamin D intake.

posts.post_title: Which acid, secreted in the kidney, is specifically…
posts.post_content: Which acid, secreted in the kidney, is specifically associated with local calcium deposition there?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Hippuric acid

Hippuric acid secretion in the kidney is associated with local calcium deposition.

This follows the general principle that wherever acid is secreted in the body, calcium deposition tends to occur at that site.

  • HCl is instead the acid cited for calcium deposition in the stomach, not the kidney.

  • Metastatic calcification may arise from renal disease with phosphate retention.
  • Dystrophic calcification occurs in mercurial poisoning affecting renal tubular cells.
  • Dystrophic calcification examples include necrotic and scar tissue elsewhere.
  • Calcification is abnormal deposition of calcium salts in non-bone tissue.

posts.post_title: Jaundice is defined as yellow discolouration of skin…
posts.post_content: Jaundice is defined as yellow discolouration of skin, sclerae and internal organs caused by an increase in tissue concentration of which pigment?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bilirubin

Bilirubin concentration increase in tissue causes the yellow discolouration of jaundice.

Correct Option Explanation

Jaundice is not itself a disease but a sign, resulting from disturbed bilirubin production, uptake, conjugation, or excretion.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Biliverdin is instead the green-blue pigment stage seen in ageing local haemorrhages (bruises), not jaundice.
  • Haemosiderin is an iron-containing pigment causing brown discolouration, not the yellow of jaundice.
  • Melanin is a black pigment produced by melanocytes, unrelated to jaundice.
Know More
  • Jaundice is classified as haemolytic, toxic or obstructive in type.
  • Van den Bergh test is the chemical test used for bilirubin.
  • Impaired conjugation and biliary obstruction are among the causes.
  • Increased haemolysis leads to overproduction of bilirubin.

posts.post_title: Jaundice resulting from overproduction of bilirubin…
posts.post_content: Jaundice resulting from overproduction of bilirubin due to increased haemolysis is classified as which of the following types?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Haemolytic or prehepatic jaundice

Haemolytic (prehepatic) jaundice results from overproduction of bilirubin due to increased haemolysis.

Correct Option Explanation

Excessive haemolysis exceeds the liver's conjugation capacity, leaving unconjugated bilirubin in blood while intensifying faecal and urinary pigment.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Toxic or intrahepatic jaundice instead arises from hepatocyte necrosis impairing bilirubin conversion, not from excess haemolysis.
  • Obstructive or posthepatic jaundice instead arises from blockage of bile flow, not from excess red cell destruction.
  • Congenital jaundice is not one of the three classified types described (haemolytic, toxic, obstructive).
Know More
  • Haemolytic jaundice causes include babesiosis and equine infectious anaemia.
  • Faeces become intense yellow due to excess urobilin formation.
  • Serum van den Bergh test shows an indirect reaction in this type.
  • Haemoglobinuria and anaemia are present in haemolytic jaundice.

posts.post_title: Which of the following protozoal diseases is listed…
posts.post_content: Which of the following protozoal diseases is listed as a specific cause of haemolytic jaundice?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Babesiosis

Babesiosis, a protozoal disease, is listed as a cause of haemolytic jaundice.

Correct Option Explanation

Babesiosis destroys red blood cells directly, producing excessive haemolysis and consequent overproduction of unconjugated bilirubin.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Salmonellosis is instead a bacterial cause of toxic or intrahepatic jaundice, not haemolytic jaundice.
  • Infectious canine hepatitis is instead a viral cause of toxic or intrahepatic jaundice.
  • Fasciola gigantica infestation is instead a cause of obstructive (posthepatic) jaundice in cattle.
Know More
  • Anaplasmosis and trypanosomosis are other protozoal causes of haemolytic jaundice.
  • Post-parturient haemoglobinuria from phosphorus deficiency also causes it.
  • Copper and selenium toxicity in sheep are chemical causes.
  • Equine infectious anaemia virus is a viral cause of haemolytic jaundice.

posts.post_title: Obstructive jaundice caused by blocking of the bile…
posts.post_content: Obstructive jaundice caused by blocking of the bile duct from within is exemplified by infestation with which fluke in cattle?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Fasciola gigantica

Fasciola gigantica infestation in cattle exemplifies bile-duct blockage causing obstructive jaundice.

Correct Option Explanation

This liver fluke blocks the bile duct from within, alongside other causes like Ascaris lumbricoides in swine and gall stones.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Babesiosis is instead a protozoal cause of haemolytic jaundice, not bile-duct obstruction.
  • Trypanosomosis is instead a protozoal cause of haemolytic jaundice, not bile-duct obstruction.
  • Clostridium haemolyticum is instead a bacterial cause of haemolytic jaundice, not bile-duct obstruction.
Know More
  • Thysanosoma actinioides (fringed tapeworm) also blocks the bile duct.
  • Obstructive jaundice may also result from external pressure by tumours.
  • Cholangitis and cholecystitis are inflammatory causes of obstructive jaundice.
  • No urobilinogen is formed since bile fails to enter the intestine.

posts.post_title: In obstructive (posthepatic) jaundice, the faeces are…
posts.post_content: In obstructive (posthepatic) jaundice, the faeces are characteristically described in which of the following ways?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Clay coloured, greasy, foul smelling

Faeces are clay coloured, greasy and foul smelling in obstructive jaundice.

Correct Option Explanation

Failure of bile to enter the intestine impairs fat emulsification and removes faecal pigment, producing this distinctive stool appearance.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Intense yellow, no smell instead describes faeces in haemolytic jaundice, from excess urobilin.
  • Normal in colour and consistency instead describes faeces in toxic (intrahepatic) jaundice.
  • Black and tarry faeces (melena) is a sign of gastrointestinal haemorrhage, unrelated to jaundice type.
Know More
  • Urine contains no urobilin in obstructive jaundice.
  • Clotting defects occur due to failure of vitamin K absorption.
  • Total serum cholesterol is increased in obstructive jaundice.
  • Serum van den Bergh test is direct in obstructive jaundice.

posts.post_title: In haemolytic jaundice, the serum van den Bergh test…
posts.post_content: In haemolytic jaundice, the serum van den Bergh test characteristically shows which of the following reaction patterns?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Indirect

The serum van den Bergh test is indirect in haemolytic jaundice.

Correct Option Explanation

This reflects the predominance of unconjugated bilirubin in the blood, since the liver's conjugation capacity is exceeded by excessive haemolysis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Direct reaction instead characterises obstructive jaundice, reflecting conjugated bilirubin excess.
  • Biphasic reaction instead characterises toxic (intrahepatic) jaundice, reflecting both bilirubin fractions.
  • Negative is not a recognised van den Bergh pattern for any of the three jaundice types.
Know More
  • Urine bilirubin is not present in haemolytic jaundice.
  • Urine urobilinogen is slightly present in haemolytic jaundice.
  • Liver function tests are negative in haemolytic jaundice.
  • Blood prothrombin time is normal in haemolytic jaundice.

posts.post_title: Which type of jaundice is characteristically…
posts.post_content: Which of the following types of jaundice is characteristically associated with an increased total serum cholesterol level?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Obstructive or posthepatic jaundice

Obstructive jaundice shows increased total serum cholesterol.

Correct Option Explanation

This differs from the other jaundice types, providing a useful differential laboratory marker along with a direct van den Bergh reaction.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Haemolytic jaundice instead shows a normal total serum cholesterol level, not increased.
  • Toxic jaundice instead shows a decreased total serum cholesterol level, not increased.
  • Congenital jaundice is not one of the three classified jaundice types with a defined cholesterol pattern here.
Know More
  • Liver function tests are positive specifically in toxic jaundice.
  • Haemoglobinuria and anaemia are present only in haemolytic jaundice.
  • Obstructive jaundice shows a direct serum van den Bergh reaction.
  • Blood prothrombin time is prolonged in both toxic and obstructive jaundice.

posts.post_title: Fagopyrin, found in Fagopyrum esculentum, is a…
posts.post_content: Fagopyrin, a helianthrone pigment found in Fagopyrum esculentum, is a cause of which type of photosensitization?

posts.post_title: Impaired hepatic excretion of phylloerythrin, derived…
posts.post_content: Impaired hepatic excretion of phylloerythrin, derived from chlorophyll degradation in the gut, causes which type of photosensitization?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Type III Hepatogenous photosensitization

Type III is caused by impaired hepatic excretion of phylloerythrin.

This form mainly affects herbivores and is caused by hepatocellular damage, biliary obstruction, or inherited hepatic defects that impair phylloerythrin clearance.

  • Type I instead results from direct plant pigment absorption without liver involvement.

  • Lantana camara and Tribulus terrestris cause toxic hepatitis leading to this type.
  • Leptospirosis infection is also a cause of hepatogenous photosensitization.
  • Sheep show facial eczema or 'swollen head' in this condition.
  • CCl4 poisoning is a chemical cause of hepatogenous photosensitization.

posts.post_title: Discolouration of bone due to accumulation of…
posts.post_content: Discolouration of bone due to accumulation of uroporphyrin in abnormal porphyrin metabolism is specifically termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

Osteohaemochromatosis is bone discolouration caused by uroporphyrin accumulation.

  • Bovine congenital porphyria is an example of Type II photosensitization.
  • Bovine haematopoetic protoporphyria is another Type II example.
  • Protoporphyrin also accumulates alongside uroporphyrin in this condition.
  • The associated dental change is termed 'pink teeth'.

posts.post_title: Complete failure of an organ to develop in utero…
posts.post_content: Complete failure of an organ to develop in utero, which is incompatible with life when a vital organ is involved, is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Aplasia

Aplasia is the complete failure of an organ to develop.

Correct Option Explanation

This developmental disturbance occurs in the embryo or foetus in utero, with rudimentary fat and connective tissue present in place of the organ.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Hypoplasia is instead failure to attain full normal adult size, not complete non-development.
  • Atrophy is decrease in size after an organ has already attained full normal growth, a later-life change.
  • Dysplasia is malformation during tissue maturation with disordered architecture, not complete absence.
Know More
  • Aplasia is one of several failures to develop, alongside agenesis and hypoplasia.
  • Genetic mutation is one cause of late foetal hypoplastic change.
  • Virus infection can also cause hypoplastic organ changes.
  • Growth disturbances range from no growth to uncontrolled growth (neoplasm).

posts.post_title: Failure of an organ or tissue to attain its full…
posts.post_content: Failure of an organ or tissue to attain its full normal adult size is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Hypoplasia

Hypoplasia is failure of an organ or tissue to attain its full normal adult size.

Correct Option Explanation

Causes include genetic mutations affecting cell differentiation and migration, viral effects, and drug-induced degenerative changes late in development.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Aplasia is instead complete failure of an organ to develop, a more extreme defect than hypoplasia.
  • Atrophy is decrease in size after the organ has already attained normal adult growth, a later event.
  • Agenesis is incomplete or imperfect development of an organ, overlapping conceptually but distinct from size-based hypoplasia.

  • Hypoplastic organs show alterations in lysosomes and inspissated cytoplasmic protein.
  • Phagolysosomes increase in size with lipofuscin pigment in hypoplasia.
  • Drug-induced hypoplasia occurs via degeneration and necrotic changes.
  • Aplasia involving vital organs like the heart is incompatible with life.

posts.post_title: Decrease in the size of the thymus on attaining…
posts.post_content: Decrease in the size of the thymus on attaining puberty, caused by apoptosis, is an example of which type of atrophy?

Thymic involution at puberty is a form of physiological atrophy.

Involution is the decrease in organ size due to decreased cell number caused by apoptosis, also seen in uterine involution after parturition.

  • Pathological atrophy instead includes nutritional, angiotrophic, disuse and endocrine forms, not this normal ageing process.

  • Senile atrophy of testis and ovaries is another physiological atrophy example.
  • Nutritional atrophy results from starvation, malabsorption or chronic infection.
  • Disuse atrophy occurs from decreased workload, as in race horse musculature.
  • Atrophy involves autophagocytosis and the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.

posts.post_title: Hind limb atrophy in horses, due to occlusion of the…
posts.post_content: Hind limb atrophy in horses, due to occlusion of the femoral artery by Strongylus larvae, is an example of which type of atrophy?

Correct Answer: Angiotrophic atrophy

Angiotrophic atrophy results from diminished blood supply, as in this parasitic ischaemia example.

Angiotrophic atrophy is caused by ischaemia, chronic passive congestion, or anaemia; parasitic occlusion of the femoral artery is a specific example.

  • Neurotrophic atrophy is instead caused by nerve injury, such as laryngeal muscle atrophy from recurrent laryngeal nerve damage.

  • Sweeny is an example of neurotrophic atrophy from suprascapular nerve injury.

posts.post_title: AL amyloid, associated with plasma cell disorders…
posts.post_content: AL amyloid, associated with plasma cell disorders such as multiple myeloma, is derived from which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Immunoglobulin light chains

AL amyloid is derived from immunoglobulin light chains.

Correct Option Explanation

Plasma cell disorders like multiple myeloma produce excess monoclonal light chains, which misfold and deposit as amyloid fibrils.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Serum amyloid A is instead the precursor for AA amyloid, associated with chronic inflammation, not plasma cell disorders.
  • Transthyretin is not the precursor protein described for AL amyloid in this context.
  • Beta-2 microglobulin is not the precursor protein described for AL amyloid in this context.
Know More
  • Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell tumour marked by immunoglobulin overproduction.
  • Plasma cells show a characteristic cart-wheel nuclear chromatin pattern.
  • AA amyloidosis instead relates to chronic inflammatory disease.
  • Congo red staining is used to confirm amyloid deposition histologically.

posts.post_title: Amyloid deposits characteristically show…
posts.post_content: Amyloid deposits characteristically show apple-green birefringence under polarized light after staining with which of the following dyes?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Congo red

Congo red staining reveals apple-green birefringence of amyloid under polarized light.

Correct Option Explanation

This special stain is the standard histochemical method for confirming amyloid deposits in tissue sections.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Prussian blue is instead used to demonstrate iron (haemosiderin), not amyloid.
  • Oil Red O is instead used to demonstrate fat, not amyloid.
  • Von Kossa is instead used to demonstrate calcium deposits, not amyloid.
Know More
  • Amyloid deposition disrupts normal tissue architecture and function.
  • Kidney, liver and spleen are commonly affected organs.
  • Sago spleen shows focal amyloid deposits around follicles.
  • Bacon spleen shows diffuse red pulp amyloid deposition.

posts.post_title: Focal, grain-like amyloid deposits around splenic…
posts.post_content: Focal, grain-like amyloid deposits around splenic follicles produce a gross splenic appearance termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sago spleen

Sago spleen describes focal, grain-like amyloid deposits around splenic follicles.

Correct Option Explanation

The name derives from the resemblance of these translucent, granular deposits to sago grains, a distinct pattern from diffuse involvement.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bacon spleen is instead the term for diffuse red pulp amyloid deposition, not focal follicular deposits.
  • Nutmeg spleen is not the standard term used; nutmeg pattern is instead classically applied to the congested liver.
  • Hobnail spleen is not a recognised term for amyloid deposition in this context.
Know More
  • Bacon/lardaceous spleen shows a sheet-like, diffuse amyloid pattern.
  • Amyloidosis may affect kidney, liver and spleen among other organs.
  • Congo red staining confirms amyloid with apple-green birefringence.
  • AA amyloid relates to chronic inflammatory conditions.

posts.post_title: Diffuse amyloid deposition throughout the splenic…
posts.post_content: Diffuse amyloid deposition throughout the splenic red pulp produces a gross splenic appearance termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bacon spleen

Bacon (lardaceous) spleen describes diffuse amyloid deposition in the splenic red pulp.

Correct Option Explanation

This sheet-like, waxy appearance contrasts with the focal, follicle-centred pattern of the sago spleen.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sago spleen is instead the term for focal, grain-like amyloid deposits around follicles, not diffuse involvement.
  • Nutmeg spleen is not the standard term used; the nutmeg pattern is classically applied to the congested liver.
  • Hobnail spleen is not a recognised term for amyloid deposition in this context.
Know More
  • Sago spleen instead shows focal, grain-like deposits around follicles.
  • AA amyloid, from chronic inflammation, is a common cause of splenic amyloidosis.
  • Congo red is the confirmatory histochemical stain for amyloid.
  • Amyloidosis may also affect kidney and liver in the same animal.

posts.post_title: A benign tumour arising from fibrous connective…
posts.post_content: A benign tumour arising from fibrous connective tissue is named using which suffix attached to the cell of origin?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: -oma

Benign tumours are named with the suffix -oma attached to the cell of origin, e.g. fibroma.

Correct Option Explanation

This nomenclature pattern also applies to osteoma (bone), chondroma (cartilage) and lipoma (fat), all benign tumours.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • -carcinoma is instead the suffix for malignant tumours of epithelial origin, not benign fibrous tumours.
  • -sarcoma is instead the suffix for malignant tumours of mesenchymal origin, not benign fibrous tumours.
  • -itis is instead the suffix denoting inflammation, unrelated to tumour nomenclature.
Know More
  • Adenoma is a benign tumour of glandular epithelium.
  • Papilloma is a benign epithelial tumour with finger-like projections.
  • Neoplasm growth exceeds and is uncoordinated with normal tissue.
  • Neoplastic growth persists excessively even after the stimulus ceases.

posts.post_title: A malignant tumour arising from epithelial tissue is…
posts.post_content: A malignant tumour arising from epithelial tissue is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Carcinoma

Carcinoma is a malignant tumour arising from epithelial tissue.

Correct Option Explanation

A malignant glandular epithelial tumour specifically is termed adenocarcinoma, following the same epithelial-origin naming logic.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sarcoma is instead a malignant tumour of mesenchymal origin, not epithelial.
  • Adenoma is instead a benign glandular epithelial tumour, not malignant.
  • Papilloma is instead a benign epithelial tumour with finger-like projections, not malignant.
Know More
  • Adenocarcinoma is the malignant counterpart of adenoma.
  • Sarcoma is the malignant counterpart of mesenchymal benign tumours.
  • Anaplasia is a hallmark feature distinguishing malignant tumours.
  • Metastasis unequivocally marks a tumour as malignant.

posts.post_title: A malignant tumour arising from mesenchymal tissue…
posts.post_content: A malignant tumour arising from mesenchymal tissue is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sarcoma

Sarcoma is a malignant tumour arising from mesenchymal tissue.

Correct Option Explanation

This term applies to malignant tumours of connective tissue origin, contrasting with carcinoma for epithelial malignancies.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Carcinoma is instead a malignant tumour arising from epithelial tissue, not mesenchymal.
  • Adenoma is instead a benign glandular epithelial tumour, not malignant mesenchymal.
  • Fibroma is instead a benign fibrous connective tissue tumour, not malignant.
Know More
  • Sarcomas commonly spread via haematogenous routes.
  • Carcinomas commonly spread via lymphatic routes.
  • Both carcinomas and sarcomas can also use the other spread route.
  • Fibroma is the benign counterpart of fibrosarcoma.

posts.post_title: A tumour composed of tissue derived from all three…
posts.post_content: A tumour composed of tissue derived from all three germ layers is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Teratoma

Teratoma is composed of tissue derived from all three germ layers.

Correct Option Explanation

This distinctive multi-tissue tumour type differs from hamartomas and choristomas, which involve normal tissue in the wrong amount or place.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Hamartoma is instead disorganized overgrowth of mature tissue indigenous to its own site, not multiple germ layers.
  • Choristoma is instead a heterotopic rest of normal tissue in an abnormal location, not multiple germ layers.
  • Papilloma is a benign epithelial tumour with finger-like projections, unrelated to germ layer composition.
Know More
  • Teratomas may contain hair, teeth or other differentiated tissue types.
  • Hamartomas are localized to the site where the tissue normally occurs.
  • Choristomas occur at a site distant from the tissue's normal location.
  • All three are developmental tumour-like conditions rather than typical neoplasms.

posts.post_title: A disorganized, tumour-like overgrowth of mature…
posts.post_content: A disorganized, tumour-like overgrowth of mature tissue indigenous to the site in which it occurs is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Hamartoma

Hamartoma is a disorganized overgrowth of mature tissue native to its site.

Correct Option Explanation

Unlike a choristoma, which involves tissue at an abnormal location, a hamartoma occurs where that tissue type is normally found.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Choristoma is instead a heterotopic rest of tissue in an abnormal location, not the tissue's own normal site.
  • Teratoma is instead composed of tissue from all three germ layers, a different multi-tissue entity.
  • Adenoma is a true benign neoplasm of glandular epithelium, distinct from this developmental malformation.
Know More
  • Hamartomas are considered developmental malformations rather than true neoplasms.
  • Choristomas are also developmental in origin but ectopically located.
  • Teratomas contain tissue derived from all three germ layers.
  • These entities are distinguished from true neoplasms by their origin.

posts.post_title: A heterotopic rest of normal tissue found in an…
posts.post_content: A heterotopic rest of normal tissue found in an abnormal location is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Choristoma

Choristoma is a heterotopic rest of normal tissue in an abnormal location.

Correct Option Explanation

This differs from a hamartoma, in which the disorganized tissue overgrowth occurs at its normal, indigenous site rather than elsewhere.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Hamartoma is instead overgrowth of tissue at its own normal site, not an abnormal location.
  • Teratoma is instead composed of tissue from all three germ layers, a different entity.
  • Papilloma is a true benign epithelial neoplasm, not a developmental tissue displacement.
Know More
  • Choristomas are also called ectopic tissue rests.
  • Hamartomas and choristomas are both developmental, non-neoplastic entities.
  • Teratomas involve all three germ layers rather than a single ectopic tissue.
  • These are distinguished from true neoplasms in classification schemes.

posts.post_title: Lack of differentiation, considered a hallmark of…
posts.post_content: Lack of differentiation, considered a hallmark feature of malignant transformation in tumour cells, is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Anaplasia

Anaplasia is lack of differentiation, a hallmark of malignancy.

Correct Option Explanation

Anaplastic features include pleomorphism, abnormal nuclear morphology, increased or atypical mitoses, and loss of normal cell polarity.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Metaplasia is instead a reversible change of one adult cell type to another, not a malignancy hallmark.
  • Dysplasia is instead disordered growth with some preserved differentiation, considered a preneoplastic change rather than the hallmark of established malignancy.
  • Hyperplasia is instead increased cell number of a normal type, unrelated to loss of differentiation.
Know More
  • Pleomorphism refers to variation in cell size and shape.
  • Hyperchromatism refers to abnormally dark-staining nuclei.
  • Loss of polarity is disorganized orientation of cells relative to each other.
  • Well-differentiated tumours resemble their tissue of origin closely.

posts.post_title: Which of the following unequivocally marks a tumour…
posts.post_content: Which of the following features unequivocally marks a tumour as malignant, distinguishing it from a benign growth?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Metastasis

Metastasis unequivocally marks a tumour as malignant.

Correct Option Explanation

While rapid growth, mitotic activity and pleomorphism are commonly associated with malignancy, the establishment of secondary growths discontinuous from the primary tumour is the definitive criterion.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Rapid growth can occur in some benign lesions too and is not by itself definitive of malignancy.
  • Increased mitotic activity can also occur in benign or reactive proliferations, not exclusively malignant tumours.
  • Pleomorphism is a feature of anaplasia often seen in malignancy but is not the single unequivocal defining criterion.
Know More
  • Routes of metastasis include direct seeding, lymphatic and haematogenous spread.
  • Carcinomas typically spread via lymphatics; sarcomas via blood vessels.
  • The sentinel lymph node is the first node draining a primary tumour.
  • Liver and lungs are common sites of haematogenous metastasis.

posts.post_title: Spread of tumour cells (metastasis) is defined as…
posts.post_content: Spread of tumour cells (metastasis) is defined as the establishment of secondary growths at a site that is what, relative to the primary tumour?

_aimcq_options.text: Immediately adjacent to the primary tumour
Within the same organ as the primary tumour
Connected by a fibrous stalk to the primary tumour

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Discontinuous with the primary tumour

Metastasis establishes secondary growths discontinuous with the primary tumour.

Correct Option Explanation

This spatial discontinuity, achieved via lymphatic, haematogenous, or seeding routes, is the defining feature separating metastasis from local invasion.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • "Immediately adjacent" instead describes local invasion, a different malignant behaviour, not metastasis.
  • "Within the same organ" does not capture the essential discontinuity that defines metastasis.
  • "Connected by a fibrous stalk" does not describe the mechanism or definition of metastatic spread.
Know More
  • Direct seeding occurs when tumour cells invade a natural body cavity.
  • Lymphatic spread is the more common route for carcinomas.
  • Haematogenous spread is typical of sarcomas but also occurs in carcinomas.
  • Benign tumours, by definition, do not metastasize.

posts.post_title: The first lymph node that receives lymphatic…
posts.post_content: The first lymph node that receives lymphatic drainage directly from a primary tumour is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sentinel lymph node

The sentinel lymph node is the first node receiving lymphatic drainage from a primary tumour.

Correct Option Explanation

This node is of particular clinical interest as an early site to examine for evidence of metastatic tumour cells.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • "Regional lymph node" is a broader term for nodes in the drainage area, not specifically the first one.
  • "Distal lymph node" would instead be further along the lymphatic chain, not the first node.
  • "Efferent lymph node" is not the specific term used for the first draining node.
Know More
  • Lymphatic spread is the typical metastatic route for carcinomas.
  • Tumour cells may bypass the sentinel node via lymphatic-venous connections.
  • Haematogenous spread is typical of sarcomas, via veins more than arteries.
  • Liver and lungs are common sites of haematogenous metastasis.

posts.post_title: Aflatoxin B1, produced by Aspergillus flavus, is a…
posts.post_content: Aflatoxin B1, produced by the fungus Aspergillus flavus, is a chemical carcinogen specifically associated with development of which tumour?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Hepatocellular carcinoma

Aflatoxin B1 is specifically associated with hepatocellular carcinoma.

Correct Option Explanation

As an indirect-acting chemical carcinogen, aflatoxin B1 requires metabolic activation in the liver, explaining its organ-specific carcinogenic effect.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Squamous cell carcinoma of skin is instead associated with chronic UV radiation exposure, not aflatoxin B1.
  • Osteosarcoma is not the tumour type specifically linked to aflatoxin B1 exposure.
  • Lymphoma is not the tumour type specifically linked to aflatoxin B1 exposure.
Know More
  • Aflatoxin B1 contamination commonly occurs in stored grains and feed.
  • Carcinogenesis proceeds through initiation, promotion and progression stages.
  • Indirect-acting carcinogens require metabolic activation to become carcinogenic.
  • Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons are another example of indirect-acting carcinogens.

posts.post_title: Chemical carcinogens that require metabolic…
posts.post_content: Chemical carcinogens that require metabolic activation within the body before becoming truly carcinogenic are classified as which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Indirect-acting carcinogens

Indirect-acting carcinogens require metabolic activation before becoming carcinogenic.

Correct Option Explanation

Examples include polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, aromatic amines/azo dyes, and aflatoxin B1, all of which are converted to active carcinogens by host enzymes.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Direct-acting carcinogens instead act without requiring prior metabolic conversion, such as certain alkylating agents.
  • Radiation carcinogens is a separate physical category, not a chemical activation classification.
  • Viral carcinogens is a separate biological category, not a chemical activation classification.
Know More
  • Direct-acting carcinogens include certain alkylating agents.
  • Radiation carcinogenesis includes UV light and ionizing radiation.
  • Viral oncogenesis includes both RNA and DNA oncogenic viruses.
  • Carcinogenesis is a multistep process of initiation, promotion and progression.

posts.post_title: Which type of ultraviolet radiation-induced skin…
posts.post_content: Which type of ultraviolet radiation-induced skin cancer is classically associated with chronic sun exposure?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Squamous cell carcinoma

Squamous cell carcinoma is classically associated with chronic UV exposure.

Correct Option Explanation

Ultraviolet light causes DNA damage in skin cells, and cumulative sun exposure over time promotes this specific type of skin malignancy.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Osteosarcoma is a tumour of bone, not linked to UV radiation exposure.
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma is instead linked to chemical carcinogens like aflatoxin B1, not UV radiation.
  • Lymphoma is not the tumour type classically linked to UV radiation exposure.
Know More
  • Ionizing radiation is another physical carcinogen category besides UV light.
  • Radiation carcinogenesis works by directly damaging cellular DNA.
  • Chemical carcinogenesis instead involves compounds like aflatoxin B1.
  • Viral oncogenesis is a separate, biological carcinogenic mechanism.

posts.post_title: DNA oncogenic viruses, which integrate directly into…
posts.post_content: Which of the following is an example of a DNA oncogenic virus associated with tumour development?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Hepatitis B virus

Hepatitis B virus is a DNA oncogenic virus associated with tumour development.

Correct Option Explanation

DNA oncogenic viruses integrate viral genetic material directly into the host genome, contributing to malignant transformation.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Avian leukosis virus is instead an RNA oncogenic virus (retrovirus), not a DNA virus.
  • Feline leukemia virus is instead an RNA oncogenic virus (retrovirus), not a DNA virus.
  • Rous sarcoma virus is instead a classic RNA oncogenic virus (retrovirus) containing an oncogene, not a DNA virus.
Know More
  • RNA oncogenic viruses (retroviruses) characteristically contain oncogenes.
  • Oncogenes are derived from mutated proto-oncogenes.
  • Tumour suppressor genes like p53 and Rb oppose oncogenic transformation.
  • The two-hit hypothesis explains tumour suppressor gene inactivation.

posts.post_title: RNA oncogenic viruses (retroviruses) characteristically…
posts.post_content: RNA oncogenic viruses (retroviruses) characteristically contain which cancer-causing genetic element within their genome?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Oncogenes

RNA oncogenic viruses (retroviruses) characteristically contain oncogenes.

Correct Option Explanation

These viral oncogenes, often derived from host proto-oncogenes, directly drive uncontrolled cell proliferation upon infection.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Tumour suppressor genes instead normally restrain cell growth; their loss, not their presence, promotes cancer.
  • Housekeeping genes maintain basic cellular function and are not the cancer-driving element of oncogenic retroviruses.
  • Structural genes only would not explain the transforming capacity specifically attributed to oncogenes.
Know More
  • Rous sarcoma virus is a classic example of an RNA oncogenic virus.
  • DNA oncogenic viruses instead integrate directly into the host genome.
  • Proto-oncogenes are normal cellular genes that can mutate into oncogenes.
  • p53 and Rb are examples of tumour suppressor genes.

posts.post_title: The tumour suppressor gene p53, frequently mutated…
posts.post_content: The tumour suppressor gene p53, frequently mutated in many cancers, is often referred to by which descriptive name?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Guardian of the genome

p53 is referred to as the guardian of the genome.

Correct Option Explanation

This name reflects p53's central role at cell cycle checkpoints, preventing cells with damaged DNA from proliferating.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • "Master regulator" is not the specific descriptive name used for p53 in the source.
  • "Cell cycle brake" is not the specific descriptive name used for p53 in the source.
  • "Genome editor" is not the specific descriptive name used for p53 in the source.
Know More
  • p53 plays a role at both G1/S and G2/M cell cycle checkpoints.
  • The retinoblastoma (Rb) gene is another important tumour suppressor gene.
  • The two-hit hypothesis describes tumour suppressor gene inactivation.
  • Both alleles of a tumour suppressor gene typically must be lost for cancer.

posts.post_title: According to the two-hit hypothesis, tumour…
posts.post_content: According to the two-hit hypothesis, tumour suppressor genes like the retinoblastoma gene require how many mutational hits for malignant transformation to occur?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Two

The two-hit hypothesis states two mutational hits are required for tumour suppressor gene inactivation.

Correct Option Explanation

Both alleles of the tumour suppressor gene (e.g. retinoblastoma gene) must be inactivated before its protective function is lost.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • One hit is insufficient, since the remaining normal allele can still provide function.
  • Three hits exceeds the number described by this hypothesis.
  • Four hits exceeds the number described by this hypothesis.
Know More
  • This hypothesis is named the two-hit or Knudson hypothesis.
  • p53 is another tumour suppressor gene governed by similar principles.
  • Oncogenes, unlike tumour suppressor genes, act in a dominant fashion.
  • A single mutated oncogene allele can be sufficient to promote transformation.

posts.post_title: Progressive body wasting associated with cancer…
posts.post_content: Progressive body wasting associated with cancer, mediated in part by TNF-alpha (cachectin), is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cachexia

Cachexia is progressive body wasting associated with cancer.

Correct Option Explanation

This wasting is mediated in part by TNF-alpha, also known as cachectin, released as part of the systemic response to the tumour.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Paraneoplastic syndrome refers instead to symptom complexes not explained by direct tumour spread or wasting.
  • Anaplasia refers to lack of cellular differentiation within a tumour, not systemic body wasting.
  • Metaplasia refers to conversion of one adult cell type to another, unrelated to cancer-associated wasting.
Know More
  • TNF-alpha is also known as cachectin.
  • Cachexia is a systemic effect distinct from local tumour invasion.
  • Paraneoplastic syndromes arise from substances secreted by the tumour.
  • Cachexia contributes significantly to cancer-related morbidity.

posts.post_title: A symptom complex in a cancer-bearing animal that…
posts.post_content: A symptom complex in a cancer-bearing animal that cannot be explained by the local or distant spread of the tumour is termed which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Paraneoplastic syndrome

Paraneoplastic syndrome is a symptom complex not explained by tumour spread.

Correct Option Explanation

These symptoms are instead caused by substances, such as hormones, secreted by the tumour cells themselves.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cachexia is instead progressive body wasting, a specific systemic effect, not the broader unexplained symptom complex.
  • Metastasis is instead the spread of tumour cells to a discontinuous site, the very thing paraneoplastic syndrome symptoms are NOT explained by.
  • Anaplasia is instead lack of differentiation within tumour cells, unrelated to this systemic symptom complex.
Know More
  • Paraneoplastic syndromes may result from ectopic hormone secretion by tumours.
  • Cachexia is a related but distinct systemic cancer effect.
  • Grading and staging help characterize a tumour's clinical behaviour.
  • Grading assesses differentiation, while staging assesses spread.

posts.post_title: Grading of a tumour is primarily based on which of…
posts.post_content: Grading of a tumour is primarily based on which of the following characteristics?

_aimcq_options.text: Degree of differentiation and mitotic activity

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Degree of differentiation and mitotic activity

Tumour grading is based on degree of differentiation and mitotic activity.

Correct Option Explanation

This histological assessment reflects how closely tumour cells resemble their tissue of origin and how rapidly they are dividing.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Tumour size alone is instead a component of staging, not grading.
  • Presence of metastasis is instead a component of staging (the 'M' in TNM), not grading.
  • Lymph node involvement is instead a component of staging (the 'N' in TNM), not grading.
Know More
  • Staging uses the TNM system: tumour size, node involvement, metastasis.
  • Well-differentiated tumours closely resemble normal tissue.
  • Poorly differentiated tumours show marked anaplasia.
  • Both grading and staging guide prognosis and treatment planning.

posts.post_title: Staging of a tumour using the TNM system is based on…
posts.post_content: Staging of a tumour using the TNM system is based on tumour size, lymph node involvement, and which additional factor?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Presence of distant metastasis

TNM staging is based on tumour size, node involvement and presence of metastasis.

Correct Option Explanation

This third factor, denoted 'M' in the TNM system, reflects whether the tumour has spread to distant sites, a key determinant of prognosis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Degree of differentiation is instead a component of grading, not staging.
  • Mitotic count is instead a component of grading, not staging.
  • Cell of origin is used in tumour naming/classification, not in the TNM staging framework.
Know More
  • 'T' in TNM denotes tumour size.
  • 'N' in TNM denotes lymph node involvement.
  • 'M' in TNM denotes distant metastasis.
  • Grading instead assesses differentiation and mitotic activity.

posts.post_title: In the TNM staging system, the letter 'N'…
posts.post_content: In the TNM staging system, the letter 'N' specifically denotes assessment of which of the following?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lymph node involvement

The letter 'N' in TNM staging denotes lymph node involvement.

Correct Option Explanation

This assesses whether and how extensively regional lymph nodes have been affected by tumour spread, a key prognostic indicator.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Tumour size is instead denoted by the letter 'T' in the TNM system.
  • Distant metastasis is instead denoted by the letter 'M' in the TNM system.
  • Necrosis extent is not a component denoted by any letter in the TNM staging system.
Know More
  • 'T' denotes tumour size in the TNM system.
  • 'M' denotes presence of distant metastasis in the TNM system.
  • The sentinel lymph node is often the first examined for nodal spread.
  • Staging complements grading in characterizing tumour behaviour.
